title: Numerical Study of Stability of Clean Critical Points across Aperiodic, Topological, and Uncorrelated Disorder
authors: Shuhao Fan, Lu Liu, Wenan Guo
abstract: Using the two-dimensional Ashkin-Teller (AT) model, we compare criticality on three non-periodic lattices: the Smith-hat aperiodic tiling, Voronoi-Delaunay (VD) random triangulations, and uncorrelated diluted square lattices. The decay of the block-averaged coordination fluctuation $σ_Q$ with exponent $α$ is used to describe the connectivity disorder. The first two lattices share the same exponent $α$, which differs from that of the third. We consider the regime where the correlation-length exponent $ν<1$, where randomness is relevant according to the Harris criterion $d ν\le 2$, but should be irrelevant in cases of the Smith-hat tiling and VD triangulations, where $αν>1$, according to the Harris--Barghathi--Vojta (HBV) criterion. For the diluted lattice, we indeed find that the clean universality behavior breaks down along the entire critical line, indicating a crossover to a fixed line dominated by disorder, in line with both the Harris criterion and the HBV criterion. In contrast, both VD and Smith-hat lattices display critical exponents consistent with the clean AT universality class, as validated by a Coulomb-gas self-consistency check, violating the Harris criterion while conforming to the HBV criterion.
summary: This study investigates how structural disorder—aperiodic, topological, or random—affects the critical behavior of the 2D Ashkin-Teller model. By comparing results against the Harris and HBV criteria, the authors show that geometrically constrained disorder preserves clean critical exponents, while uncorrelated disorder causes a breakdown of this clean behavior.
main_problem: The study investigates the stability of clean critical behavior in the Ashkin-Teller model when subjected to three distinct types of structural disorder: aperiodic, topological, and uncorrelated.
main_result: The critical behavior remains stable and consistent with the clean AT universality class for aperiodic (Smith-hat) and topological (VD) lattices, satisfying the HBV criterion. Conversely, the uncorrelated (diluted) lattice shows a crossover to a disorder-dominated fixed line, consistent with the Harris criterion.
method:
The research employs Finite-Size Scaling (FSS) analysis on Monte Carlo simulations to determine critical exponents ($
u, \eta_h, \eta_p$) and characterizes disorder using the decay exponent ($\alpha$) of the block-averaged coordination fluctuation ($\sigma_Q$).
model_or_system: The system is the two-dimensional Ashkin-Teller (AT) model, analyzed on lattices including the Smith-hat aperiodic tiling, Voronoi-Delaunay (VD) random triangulations, and site-diluted square lattices. The Hamiltonian involves two Ising variables per site.
key_observables:
Critical exponents ($
u, \eta_h, \eta_p$), coordination fluctuation decay exponent ($\alpha$), and the Binder cumulant ($U_m$).
important_parameters: The disorder strength parameter ($J_4$) and the occupation probability ($p$) for site dilution are key parameters governing the crossover regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on comparing numerical results against predictions from the Harris and Harris-Barghathi-Vojta (HBV) criteria, and assumes the applicability of the Coulomb-gas self-consistency check for clean universality.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the construction of the Smith-hat and VD lattices, and the analysis uses Binder cumulants ($U_m$) to locate critical points and determine exponents.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the critical behavior across the three disorder types, using the coordination fluctuation exponent ($\alpha$) to characterize disorder, and then applying FSS and theoretical criteria (Harris vs. HBV) to determine if the clean critical exponents are preserved.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous testbed for modern critical phenomena theory, specifically comparing the predictive power of the Harris criterion against the HBV criterion in geometrically constrained or disordered systems, which has implications for understanding complex materials.
